ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a square, and the problem gives the side length as a. The gray region above the square is enclosed by a semicircular arc with the top side as diameter, and the semicircle extends downward into the square. There is also a gray region below; its bottom side is the bottom side of the square, and the boundaries on the two sides are two quarter-circular arcs bending from the two bottom corners toward the center of the square; these two arcs intersect near the center. Reasoning: The upper gray region is a semicircle, with diameter a, so the radius is a/2, and the area is (1/2)π(a/2)^2 = πa^2/8. The lower gray region is located in the lower half of the square; the area of the lower half is a·(a/2)=a^2/2. In the lower half, the white regions on the two sides are respectively quarter-circles with radius a/2, and the total area of the two quarter-circles is 2·(1/4)π(a/2)^2 = πa^2/8. Therefore the lower gray area is a^2/2 - πa^2/8. The total area of the two gray regions is πa^2/8 + (a^2/2 - πa^2/8) = a^2/2.

raw_record.question_text: The grey areas of the square with side length $a$ are bounded by a semi-circle and two quarter-circles respectively. What is their total area?

method.method_draft: First read the diagram: the square has side length a. The upper grey region is a semicircle whose diameter is the top side of the square, so its radius is a/2. The lower grey region lies in the bottom half of the square, bounded below by the bottom side and on the left/right by two quarter-circle arcs of radius a/2 meeting at the square center. From the text, use that the grey regions are bounded by one semicircle and two quarter-circles. Compute the upper grey area as (1/2)π(a/2)^2 = πa^2/8. The bottom half of the square has area a^2/2, and the two white quarter-circles removed from it have total area 2·(1/4)π(a/2)^2 = πa^2/8. Thus the lower grey area is a^2/2 - πa^2/8. Adding upper and lower grey areas gives πa^2/8 + a^2/2 - πa^2/8 = a^2/2.
